blocks.x: Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82

It is Sunday afternoon, the 6th of June, 1982, about 20 minutes of three. And we're gonna continue talking with Benny Waters for the Jazz Oral History Project, archived at the Institute of Jazz Studies, Rutgers University in Newark. And my name is Phil Schaap. Benny, on Friday you brought you through the first 16 years or so of your life, through your years in Brighton, Maryland, through the time you spent in Haverford, through your early dabbilings in keyboardisms, your instrument that you received from your brother, the fact that you were involved with him when the whole family sort of gravitated to the Philadelphia area in a variety of activities including, you know, soprano sax duets at the church, military music as in the marches, the waltzes and various popular musics for dances, and of course the fact that you had received a musical education from him and had dabbled in looking at a saxophone instruction book and it continued. But now a different story, one that is more involved with the art we're thinking about, the art of jazz, is coming into play in your life here around 1918 with your activities in the Philadelphia area, and the one which you seem to place a very, very special accent on, the Charlie Miller orchestra. Why don't we pick - hold on for one second (adjusts recording equipment) - why don't we pick up the story right there with the beginnings of your active jazz career. You were, I guess, about 16 years of age, and you started playing away from your family, your older brother Clarence's band, and started dabbling in these units in Philadelphia. How many jazz bands were there in Philadelphia and how did they find out about you and how did you know you belonged with them?
Well, let's look a minute, I played with another group before -
After or before Charlie Miller?

Before Charlie Miller. I played with another group at the Waltz Dream. That was a very, very popular dancing, dance hall, Negro dance hall. See, I played at this Waltz Dream, and with this, with this - which I forget the name of this band now, right now. Anyway, it was a very, very popular dance hall, where everybody, particularly Saturday nights it was packed. And they, the driver, it was a trommel [?], and it was Charlie Miller to me. You know how this - it changed the way that I recommended Jabbo to Charlie Johnson, you know, and other things like 'Gee, you a saxophone player, I mean, you're a young guy, so and so and so and so and so' - so we told Charlie, well, that's the way I got in with [ ], the trombone player. And I liked it because it was more jazz. The other jobs were more commercial - my brother was commercial and this other band was a dance band exclusive. And I couldn't take so many solos because the leader didn't like it. It was, we had music, you know - you played those pop arrangements that you could buy on any popular song during that period, you understand - any popular song you could buy, during that period you could buy arrangement for small combination, big band, you know, 10 pieces, 8 pieces, 6, 4, like that. See, so - and I was doing the same thing that I was doing with my brother, 'cause my brother wasn't a jazz man exclusive. He just was a good trumpet player, saxophone player later. But this band, why I bring up this band so often - this band

seemed to be doing the things that I wanted to do: play jazz, take solos, a whole lot of solos, as long as I want, you know. That's what Charlie used to let us do, 'cause everybody liked to play jazz, you know. So that's why I bring it up all the time about Charlie, Charlie Miller's bands.
OK, some questions about that. When you say 'take solos', would they be solos the way we recognize jazz solos now? Were they melody reshapings or were they -
Oh no, they'd be -
On the chords?
Chords, sure.
How many people in the band beside yourself were taking solos in this modern way?
Trumpet and the trombone.
The trumpeter was this man Lee, Bill Lee?
Bill Lee, yeah.
Right, and the trombonist was Dri -
Driver, which I can't think of his first name.
Right, OK.
Well, I never did call his first name. (laughs)
Charlie Miller was a clarinetist?
Yeah, he only played the melody, only.
He wasn't a soloist.

No, not at all. But he had a beautiful sound. I'll tell you the effect that he had on this instrument. It was like a violin playin' the melody. To tell you the truth, I think he played a C clarinet, and that case, he could play the violin parts. [ ] I'm sure he was playing a C clarinet. In that case he could play the violin parts, you know. And that's what he was taking the effect of, just the melody, never did - he didn't even make riffs. We were the ones that made it. For instance, he would play a melody on one of the songs back there that I remember real well now, a song called 'See You In My Dreams', you know (sings), was a very beautiful song. And he could play the melody real sweet, you know, just the melody. And we would make a background in riffs, and

most of the time we faked it, things like that. And the riffs that we were playing is similar to the things that you hearing today. [ ], three-part harmony - alto, trombone and trumpet. So he was just (sings), you know, one of those kind of things. And the, we could do that very fast, we could do it real easy because everybody had big ears, you know, they could hear, see. And I could fake it and Driver could fake it and the trumpet player could fake, and we had the right harmonies.

Some of the first solos, conceived, improvised jazz solos that we recognize as such now, that we can learn about - those of us who weren't there then - through records, seem to indicate to us that the people who were really doin' it, maybe the only ones who were doin' it at first, were Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong on the disc. 'Course it was King Oliver, at least for that matter there was Frankie Trumbauer, Johnny Dodds. When you say they were taking jazz solos as we would recognize them today as jazz solos - yourself, Driver, Bill Lee - were they on a par with or relatable to the music of Bechet and Armstrong from the same period music? You must have, wouldn't you hear Bechet the early '20's?
Yes.
And Armstrong '24.
Yes.
Well, could you compare the solos of the Charlie Miller personnel in 1918, when you're 16 years of age playing with them, with the solo work of Bechet and Armstrong?

No, I wouldn't say that. I tell you why, see. Because actually as we all know Sidney Bechet and - pioneered on the soprano, he was way ahead, and we all know that Louis Armstrong pioneered on the trumpet, way ahead. They wasn't as good, Bill wasn't as good as Louis Armstrong, and I wasn't as good as Sidney Bechet. Well, because I was playing alto, I didn't have the same horn, see.
Right.

Well, I could improvise, I always could improvise. I mean I knew harmony from, just from natural ability, I always could improvise. See, that's why I didn't like to - I was glad to be with this band because I had a chance to, more so than with my brother, all those dance bands. Dance band is commercial gig, you just play the music where it is and you get paid, but I mean, even big bands you don't - even big bands, that's, I'm sure of this, but I'm pretty sure a lot of these fine saxophonists, jazz men who left these big bands - well, it's like Lockjaw and so forth left the Count Basie before Count Basie retired, I mean I'm sure that you get kinda tired of playing that music, because you don't get as much choruses. You play 16 bars, then you cut off with something else, you know what I mean? That's what I found when I was working in the big bands, you know. The only reason I took the advantage with Fletcher's band, because I took Coleman Hawkins' place. And Coleman Hawkins was a star, way ahead, and every

number had something there for tenor, see. But otherwise you don't get a chance to play. That's why Procope went back musically, I mean as far as choruses are concerned, on his horns. Procope was a great saxophone player then, on the period he was working with Kirby, you understand? But when he worked with these big bands playing first, he didn't get the chance, there was too many others. When this is, like Johnny Hodg[es] and those guys, they would favor them, see, so he didn't have a chance to play as much. So finally after years and years and years you go back, see?
Yeah. So we have you - well, wait a second, you made the comment yesterday when we were talking about blues singer over at the radio station -
Yes -

That somebody could be in a school. Would you say the solos of Driver, Lee and yourself in the Charlie Miller Jazz Orchestra, we're speaking of the 'teens now, late 'teens in Philadelphia, were of the same school or more primitive in nature in what a jazz solo was to the innovations of Bechet and Armstrong that we hear on records a few years later?

Well, I would say it was a little bit different, see. But Bill, Bill Lee could play a much, very much trumpet, a lot of trumpet, and he improvised real well in correct harmonies. But it didn't sound like Louis Armstrong. And I could play a lot of saxophone and improvise, but I wasn't copying Sidney Bechet because I didn't hear much of, that much of those, that period, you see what i mean? So that's what I'm saying, that [ ] -
Well, there's no way you could have been copying these people in 1918 because you didn't even know they existed.
Yeah, that's what I've been saying, see so -
Right -
So -

The question I'm asking you to do try to do is - if possible - is that you've got, you're taking solos, Bill Lee is takin' solos, Driver is takin' solos, it's 1918 and nobody's heard of Sidney Bechet, nobody's heard of Louis Armstrong in the Haverford, Philadelphia -
Yeah -

Pennsylvania area. Is the music that you people were playing as solos of the nature, of the school that we become more familiar with through records a few years later - I mean, when I say "we" I mean me, and -
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
Yeah, yeah -

Yeah, sure, well you see, because it's just like - you see, improvising, you don't play like Louis Armstrong or Sidney Bechet to sound good, you see what I mean? Because you can sound good without - I could even say that Bill had a kind of original style and so did I, particularly at that period on the alto saxophone. I sound more like somebody now because I came to New York and was associated with Benny Carter, worked with Benny Carter, worked with Earl Bostic, worked with Johnny Hodg[es] - listened to all these other cats, Frankie Trumbauer and all these guys like that, listen - then you got that when you listen like that in New York, it's a mecca for jazz, more so than New Orleans, you know. 'Cause it has more of a variety, you know - more of a variety of playing -
Sure -

And you adopt, get adapted to some of those sounds that you hear, automatically without even rehearsing or practicing or trying things out. But then, there, it was nobody to listen to, you had to play with your - so anybody can play, improvise if they know the harmony. See, you don't have to have no guide, you just play the harmony. If a chord is a C seven and you just practicin', use a C seven in different ways. And it may not sound like that person or that person but it will be correct, see what I mean?

Of the other bands you were playing with in Philadelphia around this period - first of all, when Driver heard you and recommended you to Charlie Miller, was that a gig with Lonnie Polk or was that just -

No, that was different, that was a gig with a, it was a dance band, I was working at the Waltz Dream - did I say Waltz Dream before? - yeah, Waltz Dream, it was a dancing hall for negroes. Lot of people would be there, see - I think it was three times a week or something like that. And we had music - see, you could buy, you could buy stock arrangements, that's when the birth of stock arrangements, you know. And you also buy semi-swing things, you know, little things by guys like, have you ever heard of a guy named Elmer Scobel?
Elmer Schoebel?
Schoebel, I got the wrong name, yeah.
Yeah.
Well, I mean, I had something of - well, he was mak-, he was one of the first to listen to negro bands, or any other band that was swingin', and write it out.
Uh huh.
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82

You know, it was things like that, see. Then - well, as far as those popular songs, like I was saying, "See You In My Dreams", that's the one popular song I [ ], "See You In My Dreams" - you could buy the arrangements for that -
Right -
For 3 saxophones -
Whether they were Schoebel arrangements or -

There was more so in that period, there was more so 2 saxophones, tenor and alto. It wasn't so much 3, the 3 came up later. The 4 came up later and the 5 and like that, see. But it was, it was started with tenor and alto, you couldn't buy for 3, they didn't have it, see. Tenor and alto, and trumpet. Trombone, that's what you could buy it for. And then all you got to do is read, and it would sound OK for dancing. But it was limit, because the leader of the band himself didn't want too much solos and things, you see, that's why, see? The leader of the band himself wanted you to play the music the way it is, and it would sound OK. But it wouldn't give you enough jazz if you wanted to be a soloist, that wouldn't, it wouldn't help - you'd stale, you get stale in that particular category, you see what I mean? And that's what I was, that's what worried me - see, I'm, that's why I jumped when I had the chance to jump to Charlie, I was happy, just like a rabbit in a briar patch or somethin', I was happy to jump to that group because I could do what I wanted to. It was that type of band, see. We, we didn't, [ ] - to tell you the truth, we didn't have much music because we could fake so much.

Well, whether it was actually Schoebel arrangements or "I'll See You In Your Dreams", basically you are making a point that there were dance bands and there were stock arrangements available, and that you were playing with a band utilizing this formula. And Driver was on the gig and he -
Yeah -
brought you in the Charlie Miller Orchestra.
He told Charlie about me. You know, like friends - like I'd tell other guys he was -
Sure -

Like I told you about the drummer here that I worked with, little piano player I'm gonna sit - well, I think it's fine, well, that's the way the news gets around finally. He gets a job through that way.
Talking about Edwin Swanson [?], right?
I think so.
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
Yeah, the piano player you pointed out to us couple of weeks ago -
That I worked with here -
Yeah.
Yeah, I thought he was fantastic, yeah -
That's who you were referring to -
Yeah, yeah, I thought he was fantastic -
He's got a whole lot there for a young guy, you know, he's not matured like all these other guys. But I mean, his ideas is, for me is terrific there, see.
Back to Philadelphia in the late 'teens. Were there other orchestras that you would consider at least some of the times jazz besides the Miller thing? This man you mention, Lonnie Polk, what band -
Yeah -
What kind of music were you playing?
Well that was similar to Charlie, Charlie Miller, similar. Only Lonnie played a little bit more jazz. See, Lonnie -
You mean, Lonnie as an individual played more jazz than Charlie Miller -
Yeah, see -
Right -

So that made the band, in some respects made it a little bit, little bit better maybe, could have been. We did a lot of work in Baltimore, in Washington and down in the Eastern shores, see. I never forget that, Eastern shore. I mean, see, I was a - I don't know if I'm allowed to put this on this -
You're allowed to put it -
I am? Well in the Eastern shore I was [ ] in short pants. And my - ah, what-do-you-call-it guy who has to have charge when you go, when you're too young to work, to go -
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
A chaperone?
Cha - guardian -
Guardian.

Yeah, that's it, I had to have it. 'Cause I was a, I was not of age. So this trombone player - I forget his name too, it wasn't Driver, it was another trombone player, and he was more of a tailgate trombone player, you understand what I mean, he wasn't - he sounded much like Kid Ory, in that type, you know. So I forget his name right now - so he was the one that went to my aunt, got the papers from the police that he would take care of me, you know. See, so at intermission I met a little girl, see. And by the way, this little girl is livin' right here in New York, and I haven't - I didn't know, I haven't seen her, she's living right here in New York, I haven't seen her since I've been coming here, I guess she'd married somebody, I imagine. Anyway, I met her, you know how musicians, girls stand 'round you, you eyeball. So I went down in the, underneath the boardwalk, we were playing in the - I think it's Cambridge, if it wasn't Cambridge it's someplace on Eastern shore, near the shore, near water, see. Most of all those places are near the water down there, you know. See, so I'm in the boardwalk, and we were talkin' and fooling around, see. So I got a whole lot of sand on, when I came back up, you know. There was sand all over my clothes, see. So this guardian, the guy who was responsible for me, looked like that, you know, with big surprise, see. So I told him that I fell down (laughs). 'Cause I had never got really well, see, so that's easy to believe you, see. So I was brushing the, brushing off the sand off as I could, but it still was some left, see. So he - but he was nice, you know. See, they had a big to-do about it like, say "A young boy like you fooling around, I've gotta take more care of you", influences like that, see. Well, that band, we used to do colleges, we seemed to be popular in the Eastern shore. And then we also played in Jersey, then we played in Baltimore and Washington. Also with Charlie Miller, we played in Baltimore and -
So you would play outside Philadelphia -
Sometimes -
with both Charlie Miller's band and with the Lonnie Polk band -
Yeah, sometimes. You know how it is, we were gigging. See, we had this - with Charlie Miller we had this regular gig three times a week and Saturday evening, Kater. But with the -
That's in Philadelphia -
Yeah -
17th and Kater?
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
But with Lonnie, Lonnie, we didn't have a regular job. But we played in Philadelphia also. But we played there one night, there one night, you know, like we called it gigs.
Sure. What was the name of the ballroom where you played regularly with Charlie Miller?

Waldorf, something, Castle or something like that. I know where it was, it was 17th and Kater Street in Philadelphia, I know, I remember that real well. And that's down in the Soho district, or what they call - what they call that district? - you know, something like Pigalle or -
Ah hah -
In France or -
[ ] or -
Well, all the chicks like it, you know.
Yeah.
Yeah, that's where -
[ ] Street -
South Street.
Hmm.
All the pimps hang out and everything, that's where we played.
Trying to say it was the Red Light district and -
Red Light district, that's what I'm trying to say. South Street, 17th and Kater was the heart of the Red Light district, know what I mean, right in the middle of it.
Now -
And Kater Street, that particular street was considered a very, very bad street, you know. You know, Kater Street, [ ].
The ballroom you were playing with the band that just read music -
Oh, that was up around Broad Street, that was north of -
Benny Waters JUMP 6/6/82
Right -
That's a high-class neighborhood.
Yeah, but you said that was, that was primarily for black dancing.
Yeah, it was.
How about the ballroom you were playing with -
Same thing -
It was for a black audience -
Yeah, yeah -
You were not - right.
Yeah.
Were you playing for a, for strictly black audiences in the Philadelphia area?
Yes, mostly.
But the road gigs -
Not with my brother, my brother, he played with rich people's parlors and things, he has a, you now, big difference there.
Right, but would the jazz orchestras, the jazz -
Well, yeah -
[ ] The Lonnie Polk band -
Yeah, mostly, yeah -
But the gigging, like on the Eastern shore, that would be for -
That would be for negro places too as a rule, see, you know. It wasn't many bands playing in the white places then particular in that part of the country.

Do you think that the jazz orchestras that you were working with that were home based in Philadelphia are playing strictly for black audiences, at least in the Philadelphia area, and primarily anywhere they went during this period, 1918, is 'cause this music was so new and really the only people who really appreciated it -
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
Yeah -
were the black people who knew about it already.
Yeah.
You would agree with that?

Yeah. At that time the negroes appreciated more than they do now, you know what I mean? It's just, it's changed now, the white appreciate jazz more. You can tell by the audiences, I play ten countries a year for the last 15 years. And Paris, it's a lot of what not negroes, American negroes but there's a lot of black people. The West, Martinique is all black, mixed up like we are here, brown, black and all colors. The Guadaloupians the same thing, we have the Africans there. You have Cubans of all colors, they have all kinds of things, you know. But I played at the Cigalle in Paris for 10 years. And if it wasn't for the soldiers, Negro soldiers, that was based in Paris at that period, you wouldn't meet so many negroes anyplace, in the places we pack every night. It would hold about, at least 250, that's big for a cabaret, you hear?
You seem to -

See, they like the other music, they like their music. The Guadeloupe have their own thing, one of them, one of the music, one of the types of music that the Guadaloupians and the Martinique folks - they had a beguine, they call it, I think. A form of, I used to play it, I worked with one of those guys, you know, by the name of Albert Livrat [?]. We played beguines, it's a kind of a - well, I don't know, got a drum beat, it's somethin' like a bossa nova, you know. More, more than a bossa nova, more rhythm, you know. And that's them, that's their music. That's the music that they do, and they have, they have dances and they play that music, and the dances are crowded with Guadeloupe people and Martinique and African and so forth. But our place for the regular jazz, wasn't many - other than the American soldiers. It sometimes would be quite a few because American soldiers were based in [ ], before De Gaulle kicked them out, you know. It's now the base in Belgiums.

Well, back to the Philadelphia area in 1918. You sem to be saying something a little bit different than you were saying on Friday - Friday the 4th, this is Sunday the 6th. You gave a stronger and more positive reaction to Lonnie Polk. First of all, he spelled his name P-O-L-
K, you know.
And Lonnie, L-O-N-N-I-E, like Lonnie Johnson?
Yeah.
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
Lonnie Polk.
Um hum.
OK. You say, well maybe the Polk band was the better jazz band, I mean where -
Well it could -
Was Miller your band or is Polk your band -
Well, it could have been for this reason, I had a clause in that, see, for this reason. I said that Polk himself played jazz clarinet, where Charlie didn't.
Right.
So maybe -
How about -

Maybe that could have made it. But wherein that part was an asset, the trumpet, the trumpet player which I forget the name now, see, wasn't as good as Bill Lee. Bill Lee was considered in that neighborhood, you know what I mean -
Sure -
great, see, on account of his buckets and his mutes and his, all sorts of stuff like that. And then Driver was a better trombone player than we had -
Than the Polk band had.
Yeah, [ ].

Now - by the way, speaking, you brought up trumpet - you know, I mentioned Bechet and Armstrong, you know, there were other people around who you might have heard of a couple of years later like Dunn, Johnny Dunn and Johnny Dunn and Joe Smith -
Yeah.
And -
Well, that was in New York -
Don Redman. Yeah, but I'm saying, they were playing solos and they weren't copying or as good as Bechet or Armstrong, or -
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82

Johnny Dunn, Johnny Dunn was a great star then, playin' as a soloist, one of the first trumpet players to play the, make big - he was on big time, playin' as a soloist. He didn't sound like Louis Armstrong, you know.
Would you say that the -
Joe Smith was the same thing, was playin' sweet, cool jazz, I would say. And he didn't sound like Louis Armstrong.

Right, the point I was trying to get at is that would you liken this New York kind of pre-Bechet-Armstrong kind of sound of jazz that you heard a few years later - was it similar to the music you, that Miller and Polk's bands were playing in the Philadelphia area? Were there people like that or was it completely different?
Well, it would, say - what you mean, bands or individual, [ ] -
I'm talking about solos, specifically solos, you're taking a solo. You're saying that people in Philadelphia are basing their solos on chords in the late 19 'teens -
Yeah, well in that -
Well, I'm saying that's pretty uncommon, now we've got records, and we've hardly, you know, hardly any solos at all on records 5 or 6 years later -
Yeah -
So I'm trying to figure out, you know, how good and how special this was, that you're saying that they're bands in 1918 were playing solos.

I was playing solos, that's what I'm say- I was playing solos, you know what I mean? See, but I was playing solos on the chords in the same principle that I play solos on the chords now, you see what I mean? See, to improvise you have to know the harmony, one way or the other. Either you're gonna study, or from natural ability, like Johnny Hod[ges] and so many others. One way you got that, [ ], so after you know the harmony, you can play the chords. A chord has, if you have a seven chord you have 4 notes in it. A "C, E, G, B Flat", OK. That's what's more common in that period, the ninths and thirteenths and augmented and all that kind of stuff - it was kind of advanced, you understand what I mean? But OK, you take those notes and divide 'em, you could do that.
Right. Well, let me come in one more time -
So you had, you had your own solo, it was no -
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
Right -
See?

I'm tryin' to find out how good the solo work was in 1918, since you're saying there was solo work. Let me give you an example, let me come at it completely differently. You know your solos in 1927 with Charlie Johnson's Orchestra, right?
Yes.
I mean, you know the records -
Because I have records from then.
Right, right, 'cause we have the records, right? Now you think, or do you think that you play a lot better than that now?
I know I play a lot better than that.
Right, OK. Now those solos are 9 years after the way you were playing in Philadelphia -
Yeah -

I mean, those are '27, we're talking about 1918. So I'm trying to get a parallel line of thinking. Now I understand that you're saying it's the same thing in that there's a principle involved of using the chords. And you're using it for solos in 1918, you're using it for solos in 1982. But something's gotta be different, I mean because you probably weren't up to your 1927 level in 1918 and you're saying here in '82 that '27 is way behind. So I mean, how good were you playing, what -

Well, I could, I could have been playin' better first thing if I was playin' alto, that's the first thing. And that was my first instrument, and I was better on alto than I was on tenor. That's the first thing. And I could have been playing better construction of harmonies and things on the alto at that period. Then in the meantime, when I made those records with Charlie Johnson at that, at down in Camden at Victor, my inspiration was Coleman Hawkins, it was that slap tongue. You can even hear it on the record, I made a break whence [?], took the slap tongue in each note. And that was taken strictly from Coleman Hawkins. See, so I was copying then. But during that period you're talkin' about, it was not the copy, I'm just playing from my natural ability, that's what I'm trying to bring out for you, to you. I'm just playing from my natural ability, and it couldn't have been better, good thing that I'm on the horn that I loved, the first thing. Like I told you then, when I came here, when I changed to tenor, it was wished on me. It wasn't my idea, it was Charlie Johnson said "He can't play choruses, and would you" - asked me as a favor - "would you change with him and give him your alto and you play tenor?" You see what I mean? See, so I could have been playing much

better because I was changed to a horn that I wasn't even familiar with, see what I mean? Very well, very easily be playing more. I don't know, people have all kinds of things 'cause I've advanced a lot by listening. But I still think I play alto better. I think I'm more handy with the alto, I still think so. Well, that's proof that I know what I'm talking from beginning back there, I'm now, today - I think I'm more handy with the alto. I do more tricks, I can get over the horn, I can even play more modern, if you listen real carefully on the alto, you know? So that's proof of what we talking about, see. So I could have been playing better then, just from natural ability and not listening, see.
PS: Very interesting point -

Yep, you see everybody created, you see what I mean? And then also everybody stole. For instance, Louis Armstrong was playing the trumpet before he was associated with King Oliver. But when he associated, got 'sociated with King Oliver directly, then he advanced in, and advanced in, from listening to King Oliver. But he was, at the end he played more than King Oliver because I - well I worked with King Oliver, 'cause at that period he wasn't playing as much as he did when he was young, see. But I still - Louis advanced from listening to King Oliver. His style is from King Oliver, that's obvious. I've seen Buddy Tate so often you'd think he's home when he's (PS laughs) - see Lockjaw all the, I saw Lockjaw in Paris, I saw Lockjaw in Denmark, I saw Lockjaw in Sweden, you know what I mean? And Sweets Edison and all them guys, [I] see all of them nowadays. But then I didn't. It was only a few, see.
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
Aaron Bridges was there always, pianist, and that's with Bill Coleman. I used to see Peanuts Hucko, I mean Peanuts Holland -
Right -
'Cause he was livin' in Sweden, and I worked with Peanuts in Belgium - no, in Holland.

(pause) OK, let's ask a question about America as you thought about it while you're in Europe. Now you never were back in this whole period, when's the first time you were in the States again after December '52?
Five years later, after five years.
Oh, you went back in '57, you visited the States in '57 or 8.
[ ] , this is what?
This is '82.
When I came back to the States I came at your place, worked two days, remember, whatever time that was -
I certainly remember that. So we're talking about four years ago as your first time back - you didn't come back for over two and half decades.
Yeah, that's right. Four years ago, that's all -
Right -
Four or five years ago.
Did you keep up on what America was like, how much of a culture shock was it to come back? Answer that both -
Oh, I could hear records and hear the guys play and you know, the -
Well, were you surprised to find 52nd Street gone, to find - I mean, did you follow the jazz world?

Well, I - see, I could buy that "Down Beat" and all those magazines, I could buy the "Down Beat" and "Metronome" and many other magazines, in particular the "Down Beat". And that kept you up on whatever was going, was happening, you know?
Would you say that just reading up on American jazz, that you were pretty much able to step right out of 1952 into 1978, that there was no problem for you?
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
I don't understand -
When you came back here, like you knew what to expect, was there -
Sure, sure.
So even though you hadn't been here for two and a half decades, for a quarter century -

[ ], excuse me. You know what I knew I'd expect - because I stayed in my mainstream kick, see what I mean? And naturally in my category I knew what to expect, you see, because I worked as a mainstreamer and not as a bebopper, not as a avant-garde, not as a free - see what I mean? So in my category I knew that I could -
So -
I knew that I could kinda not play more than anybody but I could still get there, you know.

How about the physical setup of the clubs and the way things, everything made perfect sense to you when you came back here or did you find, or were you surprised to find the way the jazz world was here in New York?
Well, surprised to an extent of tears in my eyes of Harlem -
Umm -

That just, not only a surprise, disgusted. To the extent of tears in my eyes, tears rolled down my eyes when I went to Harlem. 'Cause that's where I came up in all those hundred and some clubs down that joint.
Right. So although the "Down Beat" had told you what to expect jazz-wise, you didn't know what had happened to the Harlem world -
I didn't really, because they didn't specify particularly in that, see -
Right -
They spoke of jazz clubs but they didn't even mention Harlem.
And you hadn't suspected -
It didn't occur to you that that meant that it wasn't there. Well, you must have
Benny Waters 50HP 6/6/82
known the Savoy was gone.

Oh yes, yes, that, yeah. But I didn't know that it went that low, you know? I had no idea that it could go that low. I was disgusted to tears when I came up, came back to Harlem then. 'Cause I was raised there, you know what I mean to say?
Right.

I was raised right in Harlem, I mean my musical grounds were in Small's Paradise, that's what - see, when I first came from, the first place I came in New York, I came on New York on big time, that was a big time club. See, I didn't come to New York like many musicians, broke or searching or something. I came to New York working on a big, that was a big name band in that period. And that was a big name place in that period, Small's Paradise was easily second to the Cotton Club, it was a better club than the Cotton Club as far as entertainment. Dig, the Cotton Club surpassed with beautiful girls, beautiful displays of their things and so forth. But for the real down-to-earth - any of the guys in my category that know, they'll tell you that
Um hum.
That extra down-to-earth dancing, the down-to-earth singing, the down-to-earth - those chorus girls, Small's Paradise was the place. You had 30 or 35 or 40 people down there [ ].

So we're - let's jump back to Europe now, that's very, very interesting insight of your return here. You're in Paris now, you've gone through the German thing and you're gonna make a stay in Paris, you got the contract with the Cigalle. Do you feel a certain surge in your career as the years went along, that there weren't as many people from your era? Have you been aided - ah, I know it's perhaps a touchy subject - but have you been aided by attrition, that there aren't that many people from your period any more, that that has aided in making you like even more and more unique, music aside, that that has helped your recent discovery? Like I noticed like in Europe you've had greater successes since about 1970, right?
Yes.
Right. Do you think that that has something to do with the fact that not only are you one of the originals, but you're, you know, becoming one of the last of the originals.
Yes.
Is that an aide to your career, do you think, unfortunate as it may sound?
Now it would be an aide to my career on account of my age. But before it wasn't.
Benny Waters JOMP 6/6/82
'Cause there were others.
Yeah.
Right.
[ ]. Now it's got - before this, to tell you the truth, I'm just starting to tell my age within the last two years -
I know that -
I've been telling -
I know that, I know that -
(laughs) You see what I mean?
I know that -

I've been talking about, "(makes garbled noise) years old", something, something, you know? Or I was on the radio, I think I told you about this little joke in Stuttgart, I think I told you that one, about it - anyway, I tell everybody. I did a television show in Stuttgart, and so I was walkin' down the main street in that, one afternoon, I was working at a place called the Dixieland Mortar [?]. When I was walkin' down the main street we had to, I, some three little kids, those German boys, say (pause) - on the radio, I mean on television -
Sure -

the guy asked me, first he asked me how old was I, Mr. Waters? I told him, I said like this, I said "Now look - ummmm years old", put my hand over my mouth like that, see. Then when I get these kids, little kids, three of them, said "Hello Benny Waters, are you ummm years old?", they're copying me, you know, see, that was real funny. They was doing the same thing that they saw in the television (laughs). But [ ], I said, it may be an asset to be 80 and playing as well as I do, at least as well as people say that I do, you know.
Right.

Because I mean, that's why I made a mistake within the federation, with the Wilmer Doby [?], I think that's the jazz federation. I get a little ad in there, see, I do that myself. I say "The world's most modern saxophonist at 80".
(laughs) Certainly true.
Well, I think so myself, you know.
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82 101
It has to be true -
Well, because I mean - why I say that, because I don't know of anyone 80 years old that plays more modern. They may play more than me but not more modern - 80 years old.
I don't know anybody 80 years old that plays as much as you in any category.
Yes - well that's, so I -
You got it.
Yeah, because I listen, you know. I go out, I listen to everybody -
Um hum -
See, I -
You got it -

I know what the other guy's doing, you know? I don't miss what the other guy's doing, I can go out and listen three minutes and tell what type of saxophone player I'm listening to. And I can pick his thoughts [?] out like that.
OK, Benny, I'd like you to try to think back over the last 10, 12, 13 years in context of Europe and tell me what you think are the memorable highlights for your playing career.
Oh, remember, you mean the things that I - yeah, I see. In where, in Europe or -
Europe -
in general?
Europe.

In Europe. Well (laughs), one thing that I'll never forget - I was playing clarinet one time, used to do a little specialty on the clarinet, one time at the Cigalle. And I was drinkin' all that whiskey, I was playin' the 'St. James Infirmary', slow but I was makin' this high note on the end, you know, see. I could do it, make a note even higher than I do right now, see, because I, like I lost my mouthpiece and clarinet here in New York a few years ago. So anyway - well, I made this note, I was drunk. I fell off the stand and the stand is that high, you know. I fell off the stand and landed right on [ ], you know what I mean? But I made the note with one hand in the air like that. And I didn't break the clarinet and I made the note and I didn't hurt myself, you know? So the [ ], the
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82 102
boss on the place laughed into tears (laughs), he laughed into tears. But that's one thing I'll never, never forget. And he -
He wanted you to put it in the act, huh?
Yeah (PS laughs), well that - no, that didn't happen in, that didn't happen there, that's why they didn't want me [to] stay in Germany. That didn't happen in France -
No, I didn't say France -
[ ] here in -
Stuttgart -

here in - no, in New York, in, and I did the same thing. But if I - I was drinking too - but I didn't fall off or nothing. I tell you who was in the band, Frankie Newton was in the band after that. So I was makin' these little [ ] that I used to play, and I, at that time the people make high notes, you know. And I was saying "Dah", and they build it up that way, "Dah". And every time I'd make higher I'd go back, you know what I mean? That, it was - so when I made the climax of the note I fell right down again, you know (PS laughs). So this guy, the manager of the theater, came running out and I, success that I am, I take about three bows, you know - you have, the curtain closes and opens, you know? "Great", "successful", "fantastic". So this manager of the theater heard all this noise and applause that I was gettin' there, and so he saw it. He saw it, that first thing, he saw it, he saw that, the way I fell. He says "Keep that in (PS laughs), keep that it, Benny", he wanted me to do that every show. So I told him, so I says "No, I'm not gonna hurt myself, you know, on account" - I didn't tell him exactly that, you know, but I told him, see, "I'm not gonna fall on my butt every show (laughs) like that for you". 'Cause I said that was an accident. He says "Good, that's good!" (PS laughs). But always in France I fell off the stand, you know, I just fell off the stand -
And still hit the note -
I had my eyes closed.
Uh huh. Still hit the note, though (laughs).
I hit the note, yeah, yeah.
You said, you frequently said over the last few years that you gave up drinking ten years ago, but -
Well, a little bit more than ten years ago -
It must be ten now. 'Cause the first time you told me, this time must be -
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
I tell you when, exactly when it was - 1969, so you can figure yourself.
It was ten years ago the first time you told me, yeah.
Yeah. Well, I told you it was ten years ago.
Yeah, yeah.
Well, I gave up drinkin' on account of I couldn't eat, I [was] just losing appetite and going without food for two or three days all in New York, you know -
Umm -
Working every night, though. That's the bad part.
Yeah.

That's exactly why I gave up drinking. I gave up smoking right here in New York, right down at the same place where I was, this dancing school right - which is 46th, used to be 46th and Broadway, upstairs. I gave up smoking there and that was in 1935 or something like that. Oh, yeah, around that time - no, no, yeah, yeah, around that time period. And I haven't smoked a cigarette since -
Probably your only remaining vice is that you work too hard, huh? (laughs)
Work too hard sometimes at night (both laugh). I need to correct that too.
Would you like to make any statements about your European experiences we were - you know, this tape is headin' down the home stretch -
Yeah -
Any general commentary about your experience, you've been thirty years a European. Just rap about in general, no specific questions, just your reflections on it.
Well, the only - well, if you say New York, why - what you say, I don't understand what you're saying -
Your experience, you're thirty years a European, just your reflections on it -
In Europe -
Yeah -
Oh, I mean - I think Europe has been very, very good to me, you know? With all, and with any drawback that may come, wherein I have to work every place where

some of the bigger times guys have worked and I haven't made the money that some guys that play less saxophone than me or little things like that - life there in general has been very, very good to me. For one reason I say, I've been lucky to meet good women, you know what I mean - that's quite nice, that's for a stranger, in a strange country. When I couldn't speak the language this woman that I tell you about, we went for 15 years - she was the asset, instigation rather is the word, I guess, of me investing in myself, a certain amount of money so I could get so much money a month as long as I live. Things like that, you know? So I can't complain, I really can't. I think the European has been very, very good to me.

PS: Two-parted question on being over in Europe. The major statements made on black American jazz artists going to Europe is that you get to avoid the racism of America, A, and B, be respected more for being an artist and not just, you know, that musician.

Yeah, that could be, that could be true. Because the art is newer in Europe than it is here. You haven't been, you haven't forget - don't forget that jazz was created in America and not in Europe. European, even the greatest European is a copy of an American, somebody, you understand what I mean?
Um hum.

The greatest - it's not true that some guys over there can't play fantastic. But you can't, like for an appearance, the guys who are technique and so forth - they can't, you can't say they're better than Americans. I mean, 'cause a lot of the things that the guys are doing now with ego, Art Tatum was doing years ago. You see what I'm talkin' about, Phil?
Sure.
And so, I mean there's no one, in every jazz musician in Europe is a - not, I won't say every, there's always exceptions now, see.
Right. Well, my impression -
Django Reinhardt was just what I mentioned, like [an] exception -
Right -
But as a rule most of 'em is a carbon copy of somebody -
Right -
from America.
Well, those two things I just cited, the avoiding racism and getting more respect as
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82
an artist - are those important factors in the fact that you spent 30 years in Europe?

Ah, that racism I've seen, I think that's international, you know? They have racism here in Paris, too, you'll see, particularly now, you know? And as far as the other thing is concerned, you have to come home back from Europe, but it's, you run through a little form of jealousy. [ ] this is sometimes the musicians that play well. They don't want to work with an ordinary musician that plays as well. They won't work with [a] negro - if they work with a negro they prefer to work with [a] big name negro that can lift them up, understand what I mean? That exists, 'cause that exists with me.
Right. And for a while you weren't a big enough name -
That's right -
but now finally you are, so now you're gettin' in on - but even so it still exists for you -
That is, now it don't matter, see. 'Cause I make enough money because -
Right -
if I don't make it here I go to another country, I mean [ ], like I was saying, it's -

So it wasn't the same kind of racism as you would have encountered here in the States, but you felt yourself a victim of European bands, European concert halls in general, the jazz scene in Europe signifying using bigger name black Americans than they were with you.
That's right. Which that makes sense in a way, I figured too, commercially, maybe -
Right -
Because I - everybody knows Benny Waters, so they'd rather have the Sonny Stitts.
Right. So it wasn't just racism, it was also the fact that you were, since you lived there they'd rather bring someone over sometimes.
It was two things, 'cause I've seen it, two things because I've heard guys, the older ones, I heard [ ] -

Right. But you do feel that to - and you say even more today that there's an internationalism to the racism, that you could have a problem being a black in France just as much as here in the United States of America.
Benny Waters JOHP 6/6/82 106

Yeah, international, that's international. That's international. I mean, 'cause first they got me in the irons [?] , a band in California, I have a band in California. And I had a Mexican, I had an Indian and a white boy. I had a white boy that used to work with Jan Garber, playing saxophone with him.
Uh huh.
That was years ago.
And that was in the '40's, yeah.
Yeah. See what I'm talking about?

Right. Benny, one last little question before this tape reel runs out. When we were talkin' about Johnny Hodges in Boston and you and him giggin', you playing piano, him playing soprano, him playing piano and you playing soprano - did he play only soprano then or did he also play alto?
No, we had it only the soprano, see. That was on account of us not havin' too much in ours hands, you know, we wasn't - and then Johnny wanted to get the practice on the soprano and so did I -
Uh huh -
see.
But did he play alto at that time?
No, not in that, in those sessions.
Not in - but I mean in general, did he play alto -
Oh, that was his role, on alto.
So soprano was his second horn.
Yeah, sure, he just started on the soprano. Alto. (mike noise, end of reel 3. End of interview.)
WNYC

segments.title: Opening of the 6 June 1982 session and recap of Friday
segments.summary: Phil Schaap opens the Sunday session for the Jazz Oral History Project, recaps Benny Waters's childhood, and asks how his jazz career began in Philadelphia around 1918.

segments.title: Waltz Dream dance band versus Charlie Miller's jazz band
segments.summary: Waters says he first played at the Waltz Dream dance hall, but joined Charlie Miller's band because it let him take as many jazz solos as he wanted.

segments.title: Charlie Miller's band: Bill Lee, Driver and riffs behind the melody
segments.summary: Solos were on chords, with Bill Lee on trumpet and Driver on trombone. Miller played only the melody on clarinet while the others faked three-part riff backgrounds.

segments.title: Comparing Philadelphia solos with Bechet and Armstrong
segments.summary: Asked whether the Miller band's solos matched Bechet and Armstrong, Waters says no: they were pioneers and Bill Lee and he were not as good, though he could always improvise.

segments.title: Why big bands give saxophonists few choruses
segments.summary: Waters says dance and big bands limit solo space, using Lockjaw leaving Basie, Procope with Kirby and Hodges, and his own place in Fletcher's band as examples.

segments.title: Self-taught solo style with nobody to copy in 1918
segments.summary: Lee, Driver and Waters played original solos because they had heard no Bechet or Armstrong; improvising just means knowing the chords, and New York later changed his sound.

segments.title: Stock arrangements and the Waltz Dream dance band
segments.summary: Waters describes the Waltz Dream hall for Black dancers, the stock arrangements and Schoebel-type charts they played, and why a leader who wanted music played straight made him happy to jump to Miller.

segments.title: How Driver recommended him, and a young pianist today
segments.summary: Driver told Miller about him, the way word gets around; this prompts an aside about a fine young pianist Waters recently worked with.

segments.title: Lonnie Polk's band and the Eastern Shore guardian story
segments.summary: The Polk band played similar jazz around Baltimore, Washington and the Eastern Shore. Waters, underage, needed a guardian trombonist and was caught with sand on his clothes after meeting a girl.

segments.title: 17th and Kater ballroom in the Red Light district
segments.summary: Miller's regular ballroom was at 17th and Kater, in the heart of South Street's red light district, while the read-music dance band played a high-class hall near Broad Street.

segments.title: Black audiences for jazz in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Waters agrees that the Philadelphia jazz bands and their road gigs played mostly for Black audiences, who appreciated the music first, while his brother played rich people's parlors.

segments.title: Audiences in Paris and Guadeloupean beguine music
segments.summary: Waters contrasts audiences now with then, recalls ten years at La Cigalle in Paris packed with Black soldiers, and describes beguine music played with a Guadeloupean trombonist.

segments.title: Was Lonnie Polk's band better than Miller's?
segments.summary: Waters explains that Polk himself played jazz clarinet, but Miller's band had the better trumpeter in Bill Lee and a better trombonist in Driver.

segments.title: Johnny Dunn and Joe Smith as New York trumpet soloists
segments.summary: Schaap asks about pre-Armstrong New York trumpeters; Waters says Johnny Dunn was a star soloist and Joe Smith played sweet, cool jazz, neither sounding like Armstrong.

segments.title: Soloing on chords in 1918 versus the 1927 Charlie Johnson records
segments.summary: Waters insists he soloed on chord changes in 1918 as now. He says he plays better today, was better on alto than the tenor Charlie Johnson made him switch to, and copied Hawkins's slap tongue on the 1927 records.

segments.title: Everybody created and stole: Armstrong from King Oliver
segments.summary: Waters says musicians both create and borrow, citing Armstrong's debt to Oliver, his own six sessions with Oliver, and that he was always an alto player, not a real tenor man.

segments.chapter: Recording with King Oliver and Clarence Williams
segments.title: Which King Oliver recording sessions was he on?
segments.summary: Schaap reads out Oliver dates; Waters recalls six sessions mostly at QRS on Long Island and remembers only 'Snag It', insisting the discographies are unreliable.

segments.chapter: Recording with King Oliver and Clarence Williams
segments.title: The 'Snag It' record and the Aunt Hagar's Blues arrangement
segments.summary: Waters says he bought a record of himself on 'Snag It' in Europe and that Panassie wrongly credited Bigard on 'Aunt Hagar's Blues', which he both played and arranged for Clarence Williams.

segments.chapter: Recording with King Oliver and Clarence Williams
segments.title: Using sidemen to identify his Oliver and Williams sessions
segments.summary: Waters says if Cy St. Clair on bass is not on a date he was not there; he also names Cuffey, Ben Whitted and Happy Cauldwell, and says the dates were done while he worked at Small's Paradise.

segments.chapter: Recording with King Oliver and Clarence Williams
segments.title: Dave Nelson's arrangements as a check on the sessions
segments.summary: Waters recalls Oliver's cousin Dave Nelson arranging most of the charts, including probably 'Snag It', as another clue for matching sessions.

segments.chapter: Recording with King Oliver and Clarence Williams
segments.title: Why the Oliver dates meant little beside Charlie Johnson's band
segments.summary: Waters says he answered European questions about Oliver sarcastically because Charlie Johnson's band, with Harrison, Carter, Dickie Wells and Billy Taylor, was more advanced, and the records paid only extra money.

segments.chapter: Other Philadelphia work and the union
segments.title: Miller and Polk as the first true jazz bands he worked with
segments.summary: Waters is unsure whether Polk or Miller came first, but both were jazz bands in contrast to his brother's society work and the Waltz Dream dance band.

segments.chapter: Other Philadelphia work and the union
segments.title: Subbing with Mamie Smith's Jazz Hounds for Perry Bradford
segments.summary: The only blues-related work Waters recalls in Philadelphia is a one-off gig with Mamie Smith's Jazz Hounds arranged by Perry Bradford, and he explains why subbing jobs fade from memory.

segments.chapter: Other Philadelphia work and the union
segments.title: Never impressed by Joe Oliver; the Saratoga Club band folded
segments.summary: Waters explains he took the Oliver dates only for money. He says Oliver's band broke up at the Saratoga Club while Charlie Johnson's kept going, and confirms Joe Oliver was King Oliver's name.

segments.chapter: Other Philadelphia work and the union
segments.title: Charlie Gaines and Charlie James gigs in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Waters clarifies that a trumpeter was better known rather than better, identifies Charlie Gaines, and recalls commercial gigs with Gaines and with Charlie James of the Black union.

segments.chapter: Other Philadelphia work and the union
segments.title: Philadelphia's two unions and joining local 802 in New York
segments.summary: Waters joined the Black local in Philadelphia at about 16 and only joined New York's local 802 around 1926, when he came with Charlie Johnson from Atlantic City.

segments.chapter: Other Philadelphia work and the union
segments.title: Leaving Charlie Miller for Boston and losing touch
segments.summary: Miller's was the last band he played before going to school in Boston. Waters admits he stays out of touch with old friends, and notes Miller later headed a Black musicians' local in Albany.

segments.chapter: Other Philadelphia work and the union
segments.title: Two weeks in a big band at the Club Cadix, Philadelphia
segments.summary: Waters remembers a big band with Louie Metcalf at the Club Cadix on Chestnut Street that closed after two weeks when someone was killed outside; it led to the Charlie Johnson job.

segments.title: Studying harmony and theory in Boston
segments.summary: Waters went to Boston to study harmony, theory and solfeggio, not an instrument, and intended to earn his living playing his horns.

segments.title: Finding work in Boston through brother Herman and Joe Steele
segments.summary: The first year he worked in restaurants; then his brother Herman's Elks bands spread his name and he began gigging with pianist Joe Steele.

segments.title: Church solos, pupils and the Bowles society band in Boston
segments.summary: Waters met Howard Johnson, played piano solos in a Presbyterian church, gathered pupils, and played semi-classical solos with trumpeter Langston Curl in Bowles's society band. The reel ends mid-story.

segments.title: Reel 2 opening; gigging with Joe Steele in Boston
segments.summary: After a reel change, Schaap recaps Boston. Waters says the Steele gigs were mostly dancing, that he had no free-solo band, and that money came from commercial jobs.

segments.title: Skinny Johnson, the Johnson brothers and Joe Steele's arranging
segments.summary: Waters calls Skinny Johnson one of the greatest pianists he ever heard, names the Johnson brothers, and says Steele's arrangements were crowded, unlike Sy Oliver's, a contrast he links to Wilcox.

segments.title: Soprano and piano duo gigs with Johnny Hodges
segments.summary: Waters and the younger Johnny Hodges swapped piano and soprano at Saturday tea parties for elite Black college graduates, Hodges getting the gigs as a Boston native.

segments.title: Lamb's Club, Black and White Club and Tom Whaley
segments.summary: Waters sorts out which Boston club was which, saying he worked with Tom Whaley at the Lamb's Club, where Hodges could not yet read music, and dates the Hodges period around 1923.

segments.title: Hodges's soprano tone versus Sidney Bechet's
segments.summary: Hodges took his inspiration from Bechet, but Waters found Hodges's tone smoother and purer and Bechet's vibrato wide, while Bechet had the greater jazz licks.

segments.title: The Goofus Five's curved soprano saxophonist
segments.summary: Waters praises a white curved-soprano player on the Goofus Five records, known only from the pictures, and Schaap guesses it was Bobby Davis.

segments.title: Fletcher Henderson and Hawkins records heard in Boston
segments.summary: Waters recalls hearing Fletcher Henderson and Coleman Hawkins records, but 'Stampede' dates from 1926 and so he played it with Fletcher rather than heard it in Boston.

segments.title: Why he ignored blues records and prefers ballads
segments.summary: Waters admits skipping Bessie Smith and Ida Cox records because he wanted to be progressive, says he prefers ballads, and explains that too many chords spoil the blues.

segments.title: Listening to white groups: Red Nichols and Miff Mole
segments.summary: Asked what modern records he followed, Waters names the Goofus Five, the Clarence Williams Five and white groups such as Red Nichols and Miff Mole, who knocked him out with their musicianship.

segments.title: Rollini, Bix and the three-trombone battle at Small's Paradise
segments.summary: Waters was most struck by Rollini's bass saxophone and Bix, and recalls a battle of Miff Mole, Jack Teagarden and Jimmy Harrison at Small's, which Harrison won. He later got a bass saxophone in California.

segments.title: Goldkette's band and merging technique with soul
segments.summary: Of the white dance bands, Jean Goldkette's impressed him most; Waters argues he studied more than most Black musicians of the time and always aimed to blend technique with soul.

segments.title: Hearing Goldkette at the Steel Pier and Roseland
segments.summary: Waters places the Goldkette band at Roseland during his time with Fletcher, then heard it in person at Atlantic City's Steel Pier while playing nights with Charlie Johnson at the Paradise Inn.

segments.title: Frankie Trumbauer's C-melody playing
segments.summary: Waters admires Trumbauer's tone and economical phrasing, and sings the 'Singin' the Blues' solo.

segments.title: Scoring Hawkins's 'Body and Soul' for Charlie Johnson: a dating argument
segments.summary: Waters says he scored Trumbauer's solo and Hawkins's 'Body and Soul' for Charlie Johnson's band. Schaap shows the record postdates the band's heyday, so Waters says the band returned to Small's about 1940.

segments.title: Joining Lunceford and working with Hot Lips Page
segments.summary: Waters gives the Lunceford date as about 1942-43 and lists the many times he worked with Hot Lips Page, including Small's Paradise, the Savoy and Kelly's Stable, where he arranged for him.

segments.title: Broadcasting semi-classical music with Bowles, Curl and Eddie Barrow
segments.summary: The four-piece Bowles group broadcast three times a week for Howard's Clothing Company, playing semi-classical pieces such as 'Nola', probably the first Black band to do commercial radio in Boston.

segments.title: How the radio and his brother brought him saxophone pupils
segments.summary: Most of Waters's pupils came through his brother's bands and the radio broadcasts, including Harry Carney, who left the New England Conservatory to study with him.

segments.title: Teaching Harry Carney breathing and low notes
segments.summary: Waters describes teaching Carney correct breathing, vibrato and the 'Doo' rather than 'Too' attack for low notes, and credits this for Carney's big baritone sound.

segments.title: Carney as a conscientious student; breathing and swing
segments.summary: Waters never expected Carney to become great but says he practiced and obeyed, unlike other pupils, and explains how breathing governs phrasing and swing.

segments.title: Tired of teaching and drawn to New York
segments.summary: Waters left Boston because he was tired of teaching, had big-band ambitions, and like many musicians wanted the stamp that New York gave.

segments.title: Joining Charlie Johnson in Atlantic City and the 'Paradise' name
segments.summary: Waters headed for a big band via Philadelphia, joined Johnson in Atlantic City knowing New York was next, and claims the Paradise Ten name came from both the Atlantic City and Small's Paradise.

segments.title: Had Charlie Johnson already played Small's Paradise?
segments.summary: Pressed by Schaap, Waters admits Elmer Snowden's band may have been at Small's before Johnson's and he cannot say the band had played New York before he joined.

segments.title: Resolving the Paradise name using the 1979 interview
segments.summary: Schaap recalls that in 1979 Waters said the name came from Atlantic City; Waters accepts it is probable that the band took its name there before reaching New York.

segments.title: Why Philadelphia first: no job in New York yet
segments.summary: After a back-and-forth, Waters confirms he went to Philadelphia only because the job offer came from there, having no New York work, and was tired of teaching, which was hurting his health.

segments.title: Long-held visions of New York and Paris
segments.summary: Waters compares his dream of New York with his dream of Paris, which he reached via Jimmy Archey's European trip and Bill Coleman, before leaving for ten years at La Cigalle.

segments.title: Touring New England with a tab show
segments.summary: While in Boston Waters worked in Bobby Hargrave's tab show around Maine and Vermont, with street ballyhoo, and the show landed two weeks at the Lafayette Theater in New York.

segments.title: Hearing Tricky Sam and Kenneth Roane in Harlem cellars, 1924
segments.summary: On his first, two-week visit in 1924 Waters toured Harlem's hundred-odd clubs and heard Tricky Sam Nanton playing with Kenneth Roane on curved soprano.

segments.title: Dating when he heard Armstrong with Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: Schaap uses Armstrong leaving Henderson in November 1925 to establish that Waters heard him at the Lafayette Theater and came to New York with Johnson in 1925.

segments.title: Armstrong as fourth trumpet with no parts at the Lafayette
segments.summary: Waters remembers Armstrong sitting in the Henderson trumpet section with no part to read until his solo break, which brought the house down.

segments.title: What 'take your Boston' means
segments.summary: Waters explains that taking a 'Boston' meant a chorus played with a back beat on two and four, though he does not know where the name came from.

segments.title: Reel 3: Leonard Fields and a great little band heard in 1924
segments.summary: A new reel begins. Waters recalls a small group at a basement club, possibly the original Small's, with saxophonist Leonard Fields, who had the fastest tongue he ever heard.

segments.title: Joining Jimmy Archey's Dixieland band at Jimmy Ryan's
segments.summary: Schaap leaps ahead to Europe. Waters tells how a Brooklyn gig with Henry Goodwin led to a job at Jimmy Ryan's after he agreed to play clarinet and soprano in Archey's Dixieland band.

segments.title: Going to Europe with Archey, December 1952
segments.summary: After about three years at Ryan's, Waters sailed with Archey's band for a month's European tour just before Christmas, thinking of Paris.

segments.title: New York and Paris as the goal; Lester Young's birthplace
segments.summary: Waters says musicians think of New York after New Orleans, as Paris is for Europe; Lester Young's birth in Mississippi versus New Orleans is sorted out.

segments.title: Hamburg, Switzerland and the Archey band breaking up
segments.summary: The tour went to Hamburg then Switzerland, where the band broke up after Archey joined Earl Hines in San Francisco; Waters forfeited his return ticket and stayed with Bill Coleman.

segments.title: Could the Ryan's gig have continued, and deciding to stay
segments.summary: Waters guesses they could have returned to Ryan's, but he decided to stay after Archey's move because he had a job with Bill Coleman.

segments.title: Replacing Dicky Wells in Bill Coleman's band
segments.summary: Coleman's group worked clubs in Switzerland and Germany, but Dicky Wells and Zutty Singleton had tired of it. Waters accepted Coleman's offer, hoping the band would reach Paris.

segments.title: The Canadian pianist who told Zutty he wasn't swinging
segments.summary: Waters tells a funny story of a young stride pianist in Coleman's band telling Zutty Singleton 'you ain't swinging me', to which Zutty replied in kind; Schaap's guesses at his name fail.

segments.title: Forming a Paris band with Bill Coleman
segments.summary: With Zutty and the pianist gone, Waters and Coleman rehearsed a new band of French and Martinique musicians in Paris for a French tour.

segments.title: Not yet planning to stay: the car bought in Germany
segments.summary: Waters says he only wanted to see Paris and Europe, and recounts buying a car in Germany to ship to New York and the tax trouble that followed.

segments.chapter: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
segments.title: The French and Italian tours with Coleman, then La Cigalle
segments.summary: Waters describes the French tour with Guy Lafitte reaching Casablanca, a six-week Italian tour, and leaving Coleman for the Cigalle with Jacques Butler.

segments.chapter: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
segments.title: Jacques Butler hires him at La Cigalle, 1955
segments.summary: Butler led the band at La Cigalle in Paris, where Waters arrived around 1955 still planning to go home.

segments.chapter: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
segments.title: Passing on a Paris studio, then buying one; plans to return home
segments.summary: Waters could have bought a cheap studio near the Cigalle but still planned to return to America. A woman and steady jobs kept him in Paris, though he considered buying a house for his niece.

segments.chapter: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
segments.title: Jacques Butler's band changes at the Cigalle
segments.summary: Waters worked with Butler for a couple of years until the band was fired. Butler returned later and other bands came in, including a bebop group and the Guadeloupean trombonist Al Levrat.

segments.chapter: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
segments.title: The music played at La Cigalle
segments.summary: The Cigalle was a listening room for acts. Butler's band played swing, bebop, waltzes, guarachas and mambos jazzed up, in contrast to Archey's Dixieland and Coleman's swing bands.

segments.chapter: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
segments.title: Why he avoids leading a band
segments.summary: Waters liked six days' steady work and has refused leadership because of musicians' drinking and fights. He now works as a soloist with local rhythm sections.

segments.chapter: La Cigalle and settling in Paris
segments.title: Leaving the Cigalle for Belgium and Germany; Al Levrat's band
segments.summary: When Butler's band changed twice, Waters went to Belgium and to Germany; the third Cigalle band was led by Al Levrat, a Guadeloupean trombonist.

segments.chapter: Life in France and Sidney Bechet
segments.title: Never learning French
segments.summary: Waters admits he never studied French and gets by on simple phrases and English-speaking bandmates, but can read contracts.

segments.chapter: Life in France and Sidney Bechet
segments.title: French fans, a French companion of fifteen years, and a failed French course
segments.summary: Fans are surprised he speaks little French; he jokes about living fifteen years with a woman who spoke no English, tells a Claude Hopkins anecdote, and recalls quitting French lessons after three days.

segments.chapter: Life in France and Sidney Bechet
segments.title: Sitting in with Sidney Bechet's band at the Vieux Colombier
segments.summary: Urged to visit Bechet in Paris, Waters borrowed Claude Luter's soprano, played so well the crowd roared, and Bechet through Jacques Butler banned him from the club out of jealousy.

segments.chapter: Life in France and Sidney Bechet
segments.title: Visiting Bechet in Belgium, cleaning his pistol
segments.summary: Waters recalls going to Bechet's room at the casino in Belgium and finding him cleaning a pistol, and describes Bechet as a character and a big shot.

segments.chapter: Life in France and Sidney Bechet
segments.title: Bechet's fame in France compared with his own recognition
segments.summary: Bechet was a national hero with a bust and street named for him; Waters says he is content with late recognition and now earns good concert money in France.

segments.chapter: Germany, Paris and return to America
segments.title: Going out as a soloist in Germany, Switzerland and Belgium
segments.summary: Around 1960 Waters toured as a soloist, lived three and a half years in Hamburg and two in Mannheim, and bought his tax-free car there intending to go home.

segments.chapter: Germany, Paris and return to America
segments.title: Touring Germany with local bands; the 1963 Koblenz festival
segments.summary: Waters played clubs with local bands and big tours with an English singer. He did not play the 1963 Koblenz expatriate festival but did a large festival with 15,000 people.

segments.chapter: Germany, Paris and return to America
segments.title: Returning to La Cigalle and settling into Europe
segments.summary: A new offer from the Cigalle pulled him back to Paris instead of the States; he negotiated one day off a month for concerts, which helped establish his name.

segments.chapter: Germany, Paris and return to America
segments.title: Seeing American musicians in Europe
segments.summary: Waters says he kept little contact with the States, but now sees Buddy Tate, Lockjaw, Sweets Edison and others constantly in Europe, earlier mostly Aaron Bridges and Peanuts Holland.

segments.chapter: Germany, Paris and return to America
segments.title: First return to the United States in 1978
segments.summary: Waters returned to the States about four years earlier, after over two decades, to play Schaap's West End; he kept up through Down Beat and Metronome and stayed in his mainstream lane.

segments.chapter: Germany, Paris and return to America
segments.title: Tears at Harlem's decline; Small's Paradise remembered
segments.summary: Waters cried at the state of Harlem on his return, recalling it as his musical home, and praises Small's Paradise as second only to the Cotton Club, with more down-to-earth entertainment.

segments.chapter: Germany, Paris and return to America
segments.title: Being one of the last originals; telling his age at 80
segments.summary: Waters agrees age now helps his career, tells the Stuttgart television story of not telling his age, and bills himself as the world's most modern saxophonist at 80.

segments.chapter: Germany, Paris and return to America
segments.title: Falling off the stand while hitting the high note
segments.summary: Waters recalls playing the 'St. James Infirmary' high note on clarinet at the Cigalle, drunk, and falling off the stand without missing it, and a similar fall in a New York theater show.

segments.title: Giving up drinking in 1969 and smoking in 1935
segments.summary: Waters quit drinking in 1969 after losing his appetite and quit smoking around 1935, leaving overwork as his only vice.

segments.title: Europe has been good to him
segments.summary: Waters reflects on thirty years in Europe: despite less money than bigger names, life was very good, helped by the women he met and a retirement investment.

segments.title: European jazz musicians as copies of Americans
segments.summary: Waters says jazz was created in America, so even the best Europeans are copies of an American model, with Django Reinhardt as an exception.

segments.title: Racism is international; Europe favouring bigger-name Americans
segments.summary: Waters says racism exists in Paris too and that European promoters often preferred big-name Black Americans like Sonny Stitt to him; he recalls leading an integrated California band in the 1940s.

segments.title: Hodges's soprano as a second horn
segments.summary: Waters confirms that the Boston gigs with Hodges were soprano only, and that Hodges's main horn was alto, with soprano his practice instrument.

segments.summary: A WNYC cover note dated 3/2/94 from the transcriber, David Carp, sending the transcript of the 6/6/82 session to the archive.
